outcomes.original: Filing step: Register for a San Francisco Business Account Number (BAN) with the Treasurer & Tax Collector and file a Fictitious Business Name statement with the County Clerk. What to say: Apply online or in person for the Business Registration Certificate; fee is tiered by gross receipts (likely $55–$95 for a new small restaurant plus $4 state fee). The BAN is required before any other city permit can be issued. File the DBA statement with the County Clerk (photo ID required in person, or mail with notarized signature), then publish once a week for four weeks in a court-approved newspaper and file proof of publication within 45 days.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain a California Seller's Permit from CDTFA, register as an employer with EDD, and secure workers' compensation insurance. What to say: Register online with CDTFA for the seller's permit (free, often same-day). Register with EDD within 15 days of paying wages; this is also free and online. Quote and bind workers' comp insurance from a licensed carrier or State Fund (restaurants typically pay 2–6% of payroll). These three items are needed for the health permit and for payroll compliance, so complete them before filing the building permit.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Complete construction, install the grease interceptor per SFPUC FOG rules, and schedule DPH and DBI final inspections. What to say: Licensed contractors pull electrical, plumbing, and mechanical permits as sub-permits under the main building permit. Install the grease interceptor sized per SFPUC's assigned Discharger Category and submit the Installation Verification Form to earn the 14.2% sewer bill reduction. Once construction is substantially complete, schedule a pre-final walkthrough with the DPH plan reviewer (at least two weeks ahead) to catch any deficiencies. After corrections, schedule the final DPH inspection and the DBI final inspection; pass both before applying for the Permit to Operate.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain a Certified Food Protection Manager certificate, apply for the Health Permit to Operate, and pass the pre-opening inspection. What to say: At least one owner or employee must pass an ANSI-accredited food safety manager exam (ServSafe, Prometric, etc.) within 60 days of opening; the certificate is valid five years and costs roughly $100–$250. Apply online for the Permit to Operate with the BAN, Location ID (LIN), EIN, and proof of the food manager certificate. The application fee is $470 (includes initial inspection); annual license fee is $0 for restaurants in 2026–28. Schedule the pre-opening inspection at least one month before the target open date. The inspector will verify that the facility matches approved plans, equipment is installed and functioning, hot water is available, hand sinks are accessible, and all surfaces are sealed. The permit is issued after a passing inspection.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 63 to 225 days. Estimated government cost: $2,168 to $18,878. Notes: The timeline of 63 to 225 days and the cost of $2,170 to $18,880 are the government fees and processing times to obtain the Health Permit to Operate and the Building Permit with change of use, the two approvals in the entitlement path. These are times to approval, not to denial or withdrawal. The minimums assume straightforward plan check with no corrections and immediate scheduling of inspections; the maximums assume one round of plan corrections and rescheduled inspections. DPH plan check takes 21–60 days, building permit review and issuance 14–120 days, and construction and final inspections vary by scope (typically 30–90 days for a limited-cooking tenant improvement). Fees include: SF business registration $55–$700, DPH plan check $828–$2,207, DPH Permit to Operate $470, building permit $800–$15,000 (valuation-based), and state/federal registrations (EIN free, CA SOS entity $70–$150, seller's permit free). Not included: construction costs, architect and engineer fees, contractor labor, grease interceptor equipment, insurance premiums, or the sign permit ($300–$1,500 if exterior signage is installed). The 1999 site-history record and the three nearby restaurant approvals indicate that daytime restaurant use is well-established on this block; the critical path is building permit plan review and kitchen inspection readiness, not discretionary zoning review, assuming the closing hour does not extend past 11 p.m.
